title: Block close: the voices
hookLine: martyrs, monks, mystics, reformers, poets and pilgrims, in their own words
tomorrow: why would a man everyone wants slip out before dawn?

lines: HE STARTS TO READ, AND DOESN'T STOP.
cards: Somebody leaves a book lying around, and somebody else picks it up out of boredom. That's how this one starts. Trier, a city of the Roman Empire.

The emperor is off at the games one afternoon, and some of his officials go walking in the gardens by the city wall. Two of them wander into a small house where, Augustine says, some servants of God live.
There's a book on the table. One of them opens it and starts to read. He doesn't stop.
Before he's done, he has decided to change his whole life, and he turns to his friend to say so.

teach.h: A BOOK ON THE TABLE AT TRIER.
teach.b: The book was the life of Antony, a monk of the Egyptian desert.
We know the scene because a man named Ponticianus told it to Augustine, and Augustine wrote it into his Confessions. Follow the chain.

Antony, the story goes, walked into church as a young man, heard the Gospel read, go and sell what you have, and took it as spoken straight to him. Someone wrote Antony's life down. Officials at Trier read it.

teach.h: TOLLE, LEGE: TAKE UP AND READ.
teach.b: And a few pages later, Augustine, in tears in a garden, hears a child's voice chanting tolle, lege: take up and read. He opens Paul's letters and reads the first lines his eyes fall on.

One voice, handed through a book to the next reader. That's what this long stretch has been: martyrs, desert mothers, mystics, a cook, a pilgrim, a young nun, each heard in their own words, not in a summary.
The letter to the Hebrews has a picture for them.

After its roll call of the faithful, it says: “Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight.” A crowd in the stands, and a race still being run.
Christians honor that crowd in different ways.
Catholic and Orthodox Christians ask the saints for their prayers; other Christians honor them as elder brothers and sisters in faith. Either way, the chain only works if somebody opens the book.

how: Christians read the saints' own writings in different ways: as daily reading, in study groups, and in the readings some churches set for saints' days; Catholic and Orthodox Christians also ask the saints for their prayers.

o: the end of a long stretch of saints' own voices
a final exam on the lives of the saints
the last service before a church building closes

games.q: the chain of readers — tap the pairs.
p: heard the Gospel as if spoken to him
told the Trier story to Augustine

s: the officials at Trier went looking for a holy book
they wandered into a house on a walk and found it on the table.
Augustine heard the Trier story before his garden moment
Ponticianus told it to him; the garden comes a few pages later in the Confessions.
honoring the saints is only a Catholic thing
Catholic and Orthodox Christians ask their prayers; other Christians honor them as elder brothers and sisters in faith.

games.q: a friend finishes a saint's book you lent her and asks, "ok, what's next?" what would the Trier story point you toward?
o: hand her a list of the top ten saints to get through.
ask which line stayed with her, and find more of that voice.
tell her a summary of the rest is enough from here.
games.why: the chain moved one voice and one book at a time: Antony to Trier, Trier to Augustine. a line that stays is a door into that voice.

practice: Find a pen and something to write on. Write the name of the one voice from this stretch that stayed with you, and under it the one line of theirs you still remember, even half of it.
That's the book to open next; if you pray, you can give thanks for that witness as you write.

wordCard.voice: Block close. The saints and teachers, heard in their own words: a chain of readers, each handing one voice to the next.

orig.note: Latin: take up and read, the child's chant Augustine heard in the garden.

carryVoice: Your line: keep reading them. Every one of them was once somebody's book on a table. Until tomorrow.
